analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "We'll hear argument now in number 861021, Carnegie Mellon University v. Maurice B. Cohill. Mr. DeForest, you may proceed whenever you're ready. Chief Justice, it may it please the Court. The issue before the Court in this case is whether a district court has the authority to remand a properly removed case to the state court for a reason not set forth in 28 U.S. Code Section 1447C. In this case, the reason for the remand was because the plaintiffs voluntarily amended the complaint after removal to federal court to delete the federal cause of action which had provided the basis for removal. I would first, in my argument, review the procedural history of this case since it is a procedural case, then discuss the statutory framework, this Court's decision in Thermatron, which we believe is controlling, and this Court's decision in the Gibbs case, and finally the various policy and statutory considerations that we urge the Court follow in determining that it is not appropriate to create a judicial mechanism for remand beyond that set forth in the applicable statute. This case arose in the State Court of Common Pleas of Allegheny County. It was filed by William and Kerry Boyle against Carnegie Mellon University, Mr. Boyle's former employer, and John Kortesich, Mr. Boyle's former supervisor. The claim filed in the State Court alleged that Mr. Boyle's discharge and the university's refusal to rehire him violated the federal statutes prohibiting age discrimination, the state statutes prohibiting age discrimination, the state tort and contract principles, and had a claim in there for Kerry Boyle, which was, she is Mr. Boyle's wife, and her claim was derivative of Mr. Boyle's claims for the alleged injury to the marriage and loss of consortium, etc. The case was timely removed, and there was no contest by the plaintiffs as to the propriety of the removal at that time. An answer was filed. The district court set a discovery schedule of five months. Discovery proceeded. Shortly before the termination of that discovery period, the plaintiffs sought and obtained an extension of the discovery period for an additional two months. Shortly before the conclusion of that discovery period, the plaintiffs filed a motion to amend the complaint to delete inter alia, the federal cause of action, and seeking a remand to the State Court of Common Pleas of Allegheny County. This was filed seven months after the case had been in litigation in the federal district court. The district court accepted briefs, and more than a year after the case had been in federal court, remanded it, issued an order of remanding to the State Court of Common Pleas of Allegheny County. The federal court held that the case had, in fact, been properly removed, and, in fact, held that Section 1447C of Title 28 provided no basis for the remand. The district court also recognized the clear implication the court described as an implication, we believe it is a holding, of the Thermatron decision that prohibited such remands, but the district court nevertheless determined it would remand the case. The district court held that it would not grant review as a certification under Section 1292 for an appeal, and stated the reason for that was because review was available pursuant to a writ of mandamus under the court's Thermatron opinion. We filed both an appeal and a petition for writ of mandamus in the United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit. The Third Circuit dismissed the appeal holding that was not a proper vehicle for review of the determination by the district court. The Third Circuit did, in fact, set the mandamus petition down for review by a merits panel. The merits panel, by a two-to-one vote, held that the district court aired. The Thermatron decision this court was controlling, and, in fact, there had been no reason for remand of this action as provided under Section 1447C, and accordingly issued a writ of mandamus. The petition for rehearing was filed. The court and bank accepted rehearing, and under their internal operating procedures, vacated the panel opinion. In the Third Circuit, their grant of rehearing vacates the panel opinion. The Third Circuit heard the case in bank, and by a five-to-five vote, divided equally on the issue, did not issue an opinion, and accordingly denied the writ of mandamus. Mr. DeForest, what do you say the district court should have done with this case and the posture in which it was when it ruled? Your Honor, we had held that the district court, or urged the district court to retain the case. Assuming the district court determined that it would not retain the case, it should have dismissed the action without prejudice. And if it had retained the case, it should have just gone on and decided all the state law questions? Yes, Chief Justice. If it determined appropriate to retain the case, it could have decided the state law questions. They were all pendent claims arising out of a common nucleus of operative fact with the federal claim. They all were those from Mr. Boyle's discharge and universities refused. Well, was there any federal claim left at that point? No, Justice Brennan. The state law claim. Once the permission was given to the plaintiff to voluntarily delete the federal claim, there were only remaining state law claims. Well, there's some question whether it could have retained the case under the constitutional grant of power. Justice Scalia, I believe, and it's clear that Section 1441A and B provide that these actions may be removed. And under this court's holding in United Mine Workers v. Gibbs, both the federal claim and pendent state claims are part of one constitutional case. And that under the statute, it is, I think, clear that as one constitutional case, the district court had the power to dispose of that case once it had accepted the remand. Well, it's a constitutional case when it's removed, because there's a federal question in it when it's removed. But once the federal question is excised, how can you say that there's a case or controversy any longer arising under the laws of the United States? Justice Scalia, the court, this court in the case of St. Paul Indemnity and Casualty Company, has, I believe, addressed that issue and held that an amendment after removal is not a basis for the defeating of removal jurisdiction once it has attached. And we believe that Congress had an appropriate power to permit under 1441A the federal courts to take these cases. Similarly, in the Gibbs case itself, this court made clear that there can be situations in which the district court may determine to retain a case, even notwithstanding dismissal of a federal claim. And I think, Justice Scalia, in the Gibbs case itself, the facts in Gibbs, if we look at them, were a situation where there was a Section 303 claim under the Labor Management Relations Act, as well as some state law claims. And the court, I believe, in that case, on the facts of it, held that, notwithstanding the fact that the federal claim properly was dismissed, that a jury verdict on the state law claims could have been maintained on a procedural ground. In that case, because of this court's interpretation of the Norris-LaGuardia Act, they found that the Norris-LaGuardia Act would have precluded that particular type of cause of action. So, in my judgment, Congress did appropriately determine that these cases could be maintained and disposed of. In fact... Mr. Forrest, what is the sole reason that you can't get in the federal court from a state court? The sole reason? It's because you have a federal question, isn't it? Is that the sole reason? The only reason? Justice Marshall, I believe that diversity cases can go to the federal court. I'm talking about a removal case. The only way you can remove it is because you have a federal question. You can remove a diversity case, Justice Marshall. Well, this is not a diversity case. This was not a diversity case. So the only reason for removal was a federal question. In this case? In this case, the basis for removal was a federal question. And that was removed? That was... It was removed after the case went over to the federal district court. Then it was removed. The federal question was removed. Well, non-procedure, would it go back? Well, Justice Marshall, there's two questions. One, whether or not the federal court can keep the case. And secondly, what it should do with it if it determines it should not keep the case. Those are two separate issues. In what grounds would they keep it? Well, Justice Marshall, this court's decision in Gibbs does indicate that in some situations that the federal courts can keep it. I would also say that this court's decision in the St. Paul and indemnity and casualty case, where there was an amendment after the removal of the case to reduce the amount of the damages claimed below the jurisdictional amount, so there was no longer a federal jurisdiction, this court held that that amendment could not and would not defeat jurisdiction. So the court has addressed this issue previously and held, and I think there's longstanding law on this issue that the federal court, if it determined appropriate, would have had jurisdiction. Now... Mr. Forrest, a long time ago, someone asked you what the court should do, and among the options, you stated it should dismiss. I think it had that option, huh? Um... Justice. Without prejudice. Without prejudice to what? Without prejudice to if the plaintiffs sought to attempt to restate those claims again. Suppose the statute of limitations is run. Justice, if, in fact, the statute of limitations had run... It's just as hard luck, huh? Well, I suggest that that's one factor the district court might want to consider in determining whether or not to dismiss the case or to keep it. I... It is not crucial to my position that the federal court... Order remanded. Excuse me? Order remanded. Well, my position on that, which I'd like to address right now, is that the statutes on remand have very clearly specified, over a long history, more than 100 years, the basis on which cases may properly be remanded. Where do you find the express statutory authority for the court? Who dismissed the case after removal? Justice O'Connor, I believe that under this court's decision in United Mine Workers v. Gibbs, that was an option available to the district court. Now, I... It certainly isn't based on any express statutory provision, is it? Justice O'Connor, I believe that the court's decision in Gibbs was not based on a statutory provision. And I would like to indicate that... So similarly, perhaps the option is open to remand or dismiss. Justice O'Connor, I'd like to address that. It seems to me that there are several factors that are crucial here. First of all, removal jurisdiction is purely a creation and a creature of statute, and remand is purely a creation and creature of statute. If the court determines in this case that there's some sort of general power, that's a very far-reaching issue. In my judgment, not limited to removal cases, because if you're going to create some power, I don't know how you would say it's limited to removal cases. But the removal statutes themselves, you have a long history of very careful delineation of bases in which to permit remand. You don't have that in the Gibbs-type situation. Secondly, Gibbs and the Gibbs decision arises based on a long-standing traditional power of the court to dismiss cases. And this court, in the case of Link v. Wabash, made very clear that that is an inherent and deep-rooted power in district courts. We also have federal rules that provide for dismissals. We have no such counterpart in the remand area. In fact, we have direct contrary congressional intent in the removal area, because it specifically provides very limited situations, only two in which remand may be permitted under the removal statutes. Those two situations are set forth in Section 1447C, if the case was, in fact, removed improvidently and without jurisdiction. Not applicable here. Secondly, Congress set forth in Section 1441C a power, a discretionary power. Congress clearly knew how to set forth a power if they wished it to be there. They set it forth in Section 1441C for a discretionary power whenever you had a case in which there were separate and independent claims removed. Well, is there any real disagreement about the inapplicability of 1447C and 1441C here? I don't think there is, Pastor. I don't think there is either, and I wonder why you're dwelling on it so. Well, because I suggest to you, by the fact that Congress has provided in Section 1441C for a discretionary power, they very clearly knew how to create this power. They did not provide it in any other area. Now, I would also urge that there are very strong policy judgments and questions that arise. Remand is not the functional... You're saying that they would not have needed 1441C if there were a general power to remand anyway. That is correct, and I also say... Especially since they don't mandate remand, but just put it within the Court's discretion. You wouldn't need that at all. And I also say it indicates very clearly in their mind that they knew they could do it if they wished to. It wasn't just something in the back of their mind. Here they did it in another section of the statute. So 1441C makes it pretty clear they knew how to do it if they wanted it done. And it's important to remember, in my judgment, that removal, and this Court in the Shamrock Oil and Gas case made very clear the removal area because of a long history of statutory regulation. In fact, the Court said, I quote, The policy of the successive acts of Congress regulating the jurisdiction of the federal courts is one calling for strict construction of such legislation. We are dealing here in the removal area with interpretation of legislation. We are dealing with interpretation of legislation which also contains in it a discretionary power when Congress wished it to be here. Well, we're also dealing, aren't we, with interpretation of Thermtron. Yes, yes, Justice. Because obviously the courts and the justices below go off in all directions. I'd like to address that, if I might, for a second here. This Court's opinion... Thermtron certainly doesn't control this case. That was a diversity case. This is a pending claims case. Thermtron was a case in which I don't believe it was diversity. I believe it was a case in which there was a remand for reason of a judge saying that there was a crowded docket. Now, I understand there was a diversity aspect to the case, but my view of it is that the Court... No, I agree. It was a diversity... It was initially a diversity... It was a diversity case. Yes, sir. That's why it was removed. Yes, but I was going to say that this Court's decision was not in any way conditioned upon the fact that it was a diversity case. The Court said that... Well, the fact is we didn't have a federal question case before us. Well, I would urge the Court, where Congress has patched a statute that says a diversity case is removable, that there is just as much a right in that situation to somebody to be in federal court as if the Congress had passed a statute saying age discrimination is illegal. So I personally believe both the jurisdiction for diversity cases and the jurisdiction for age discrimination cases is conditioned upon congressional statute, Justice. And that's why I was saying that I don't believe that the fact that there was a diversity there was contingent... It was a factor in the determination that the Court said. There's a difference in that the reason why I was in federal court survived and still existed at the time of the remand, which isn't true here. Yes, that... I mean, that doesn't make any difference, but at least a difference. There is a difference there, Justice. And I would address that by saying that, obviously, there are many reasons why claims, whether they be initial federal claims under federal statutes or diversity statutes, are removed from cases. And this Court dealt with one in Gibbs, where, in fact, the federal claim was, in fact, held. It was dismissed, but it was also held that a state court's judgment could have been maintained. In that case, it determined not to do it for reasons of interpretation of the Norris LaGuardia Act. So my suggestion is that there is, in fact, that factor, but I don't think it is a distinction. It is... The next thing about discretion, which I guess you're talking about... Do you think that the district court would have had discretion to grant a motion to abstain, pending the plaintiff's attempt to refile and get a ruling on the statute of limitations question in the state court, and then just hold the case until it finds out what happens in the state court and then dismiss? Justice... Either dismiss or then go ahead and try it. Justice Stevens, I don't believe that that type of abstention is authorized under any of the abstention doctrines that I'm familiar with under Younger or Pullman or Burford, and I don't believe that that would be an appropriate type of abstention, in my opinion. And... Let me judge it. It would have the power to do that? Maybe it hasn't been done before, but is there anything that would restrict its power to do that? It would be creating a new basis for abstention, Justice, and I guess if you wanted to do it, you probably... The court probably could, but... So I can't say that you can't create it, but it doesn't seem to me to be... As a practical matter, any administration of cases have to deal with many different contingencies and factors, and they make many... There's one consideration. Federal judges, if they can get state judges to decide state law issues, they kind of like to do it that way. I can understand that, Justice, but it seems to me that the basic... So I suppose that there could be an abstention for the purpose of... And the question they might be uncertain about is whether the statute of limitations had run, and, you know, so... I suppose it's... They can't hold the case on the docket until they can find out. I suppose that's a possibility, Justice, although, frankly, it's not within any of the documents of abstention, which I'm... The plaintiffs did. They deleted in one... At the same time, deleted the federal claim and moved to have it remanded to state court. And why is it worth your time to argue that, well, the judge could have gotten rid of the case, but if he wanted to get rid of it, he had to dismiss it rather than remand it? Well, are you asking a practical question or a question of statutory interpretation? I'm asking why you're... Because we feel... Why was it worth a while for your client... Because... ...to send you up here on a petition? Yes. As a practical matter, there are several factors. One of which is that this case, in our judgment, would have been and should have been tried shortly. And in our... With one month left... Well, it may be, but you say the judge could have gotten rid of the case. He wasn't required to keep it. I'm attempting to say to you... Oh, I know. Isn't that your position? That he wasn't required to keep it. He could have dismissed it. I believe that under this court's Gibbs, he probably had the discretionary power. I'm not saying that he should have done it. In fact, I would... Right. If I were a district court judge, I don't believe that I would have done it, and I don't think this judge would have done it. Well, it may be. Now, go ahead. What are the... What are the other... Well, what I'm saying to you is, I don't think that the district judge would have dismissed it. I think that he would have kept the case, and we would have had a trial. That's my... You're asking me the practical consequence of why... What the process that I went through, or we go through in our mind here, that if he doesn't have an option to remand, I don't think he's going to dismiss it. I think that he probably would have kept the case and tried it. Why wouldn't he? Because I think he probably would have been concerned about these statute of limitations issues. Well, was it arguably barred by the statute or not? Some of the claims would have been justice. Right. In my opinion. Well, I can understand why you didn't want to remand. Was that one of the reasons? Well, I'm telling you our reason. We felt we would get a trial, and that's what... That is... That was our reason, and we thought it would have been appropriate. But I'm... As a matter of statutory interpretation, which I believe is really the crucial issue, in my opinion here, that we have the question of whether, under the removal statutes, this court is going to create a power that does not exist clearly under the statutes now, and where that power is going to come from. And we've... I've urged all the reasons why I think, as a matter of statutory interpretation, that in looking at the legislation, in my opinion, it would be inappropriate for the court to do so. I would like to suggest that the Gibbs case itself does not provide an independent power, which is what the district court seemed to feel. And that's another avenue here. Even assuming that the court were not going to follow the strict interpretation of the removal statute, you'd still have to face the question, where does this power to remand come from? And... Forrest, what is a remand? Is it a... Is it a... Is it a mandate by a federal court? If I'm a state court judge and I get a remand case, can I decline to entertain it? I mean, is it just a request to a state court to entertain it, or is the state court bound to entertain it on remand as owed? Well, Justice, I... I think it's in order, but... I'm not a state court judge either, and... And I don't know exactly... The court started off is in the state court. Yes. Yes. But what... So I don't know whether there's some situations that a state court judge might say, well, I won't take it, if that's what... Yeah, I'm wondering if a state court judge says, I won't take it for whatever reason. You'll have to refile and take your chances with a statute of limitation. I wonder whether that's in violation of a federal court order that... I... In my opinion, I think it would be, but again, I don't know that that's... That I've ever seen that. You're actually creating a new rule of law when you say it violates a federal statute? Nothing in the federal statute says they have to take it. Justice, I'm... I don't know. I'm not for creating a new rule. Well, you seem to be on what the judge wants to do. I guess he just makes it up as he goes along. I... I don't know what the state court judge is going to do, Justice. And the statute doesn't tell us the answer to that question, you're saying? I don't think it does, in my opinion. On the reason, Congress must have thought some judges had to do a little filling in of holes in the statute, I suppose. Well, I think perhaps, but I think that if you're alluding to this issue, this issue is clearly addressed by Congress, one, within their contemplation, and I think there's a very different issue when you have an area that Congress has specifically addressed, as they have here, both under 1447C and 1441C. I would like to discuss briefly... No, you may have covered it, but I want to be sure I have your answer. What is the source of the district court's power to dismiss the case? I believe that the district court probably would have discretion in the application of the Gibbs factors. Yeah, but what is the... Before Gibbs was decided, say this came up. Well, that power has been recognized in this court for a long time. It goes back to the case of Osborne versus the Bank of U.S., Chief Justice Marshall. And that power, before that, it comes from the inherent power that this court recognized in the case of Link versus Wabash Railroad of non-suit and non-prosecuteur at the common law. There's inherent power to dismiss a case like that, but there's no inherent power to remand it. I think that's correct. Remand is very specifically a creation of statute, and this court is so held, both in the shamrock, oil, and gas case. And I believe, if you look at the St. Paul and Demony in casualty case, where they say once you get the jurisdiction of the federal court, that the plan of subsequent amendments cannot remove it. I would just like to say two or a few policy considerations. One, it seems clear to me that Congress knew how to create this power, did so in certain sections of the statute, did not create it here. Secondly, that if this court would create such a power, it would make meaningless the creation of that power to remand set forth and the limitations in sections 1447c and in 1441c. It would also, in my opinion, create an unwieldy situation in the district courts where these district courts now, contrary to the rule of this court in Thermatron and in the case of Gravid versus Southwestern Bell, where the courts said we're not, the courts, the appellate courts, aren't to get into reviews here of these things. They just determine whether there's a power there. But once we create this additional power, non-statutory power to remand, we're now saying to the circuit courts, you're going to have to somehow administer that. We're going to embroil the circuit courts, in my opinion, in mandamus review over actions. And if they aren't embroiled in that, there will be no appellate review at all of these. By circuit court, you mean court of appeals? Is that what you're talking about? Yes, yes, Justice. And finally, it can lead to the possibilities of manipulation of the forum, as well as, in my opinion, needless delay and duplicative... Can't the district judge supervise and control alleged manipulation? He knows when counsel are manipulating. Well, Justice, I'm not sure that you can tell what someone's reason for doing something is in their mind. I mean, I think I'm just saying that where somebody wants to get out of federal court, it's going to be very easy to do under this power. I want to go back to your comment, too, about you don't know what a state court judge is going to do. The state court judge has nothing to do with removal at all, does he? If a petition for removal is filed, the case is removed. And any issue of the propriety of removal is a federal court issue, not a state court issue. So if the case is remanded, the state court judge merely finds it back in his files again. Of course he's going to trial. I didn't say he wasn't. Someone asked me if, in fact, he could refuse to trial, or if it would be a violation of a court order, and I don't know the answer to that. I'd like to reserve whatever time I have. Thank you, Mr. DeForest. We'll hear now from you, Mr. Opsetnik. Mr. Chief Justice, and if it please the court, while the district court has clearly the ability to hear or dismiss pendant state claims, I believe also the court has the power, as in this case, to remand those pendant state claims and return them to the state court. This case, unlike the situation in Thermtron, is a pendant jurisdiction case. It's a federal law claim linked with certain state law claims that arise from a common nucleus of operative fact. There's been no debate to that point. As a result, this case is controlled by the doctrine of pendant jurisdiction that began, I believe, as Mr. DeForest said, with the Oswald or the Osborne case in the 1800s, and it was most recently discussed by this court in the Gibbs case. You do have some rather strong intimations in the St. Paul Mercury case to overcome, don't you, where they say that the fact that the district court couldn't dismiss the case means a for sure, it couldn't remand it, that the authority to remand is more strictly construed and more circumscribed than the authority to dismiss. I think that rule is clear, Mr. Chief Justice. However, the policy of strictly construing removal statutes would, I believe, in this case, even reinforce the decision of the district court, that removal is limited and that this case, because there is no federal issue at this point in time, should be returned to the state court. Well, St. Paul doesn't say removal should be strictly more strictly. It says remand should be more strictly construed. And you're saying it should be remanded. Yes, Your Honor. The, I guess the best answer to that would be the analysis in Gibbs, which came after St. Paul, lays out certain elements that have to be adhered to for the court to retain jurisdiction. There has to be an analysis of judicial economy, convenience, and fairness to the litigants. Chief Judge Cohill in the district court made that analysis in this case, found that the case when the federal claim was deleted was, there were no other federal claims. The state claims predominated. The case was not at the point of trial. And the state claims that remained would not implicate any important federal policy. He therefore remanded the case in line with Gibbs, even though Gibbs, since it was not a removed case, dealt strictly with dismissal without prejudice as opposed to remand. Counsel, it may be utterly irrelevant, but what is the state of the state court calendars in Pittsburgh? Justice Blackman, the civil calendar in the Court of Commerce, please the Valley and County. It's such that from when a case is, the phrase is placed at issue, it would be approximately 18 months before the case was listed for jury trial. And how does that compare to the federal calendar? I don't think there's any doubt that this case would be tried faster in federal court than if it were returned to state court. Obviously, we were willing to, we on behalf of the plaintiffs in this case, were willing to take a little more time. We did not factor in this two-plus-year detour to this honorable court. Justice White, the federal issue was raised in the complaint. The complaint was filed shortly before the one-year statute of limitations on the state defamation claim had expired. Upon preparation for the depositions of plaintiff and his wife, we determined that both procedurally and, in fact, the allegation of age discrimination under the Age Discrimination Employment Act simply was not viable. That the factual thrust and where plaintiffs will succeed if they do succeed is solidly on a just common law of Pennsylvania employment wrongful discharge case. At that point, shortly after the depositions were taken of the plaintiffs is when the motion to amend the complaint to delete the federal age discrimination claim, a very similar state age discrimination claim, state common law defamation claim, and certain consortium allegations was deleted. If you're the plaintiff in this case and you're in federal court by virtue of the removal, you have an opportunity to get to trial in federal court in a couple months and you're going to wait a lot longer in state court, why isn't it to the plaintiff's interest to have it tried in the federal court? Three reasons, I believe, Mr. Chief Justice. One, the state court system would provide for quite possibly a settlement that would be favorable to the plaintiffs. You mean compulsory arbitration or something like that? Not compulsory arbitration. Simply the state court, given their crowded, by comparison crowded civil schedule, I think exercise is much more pressure. Pressure. Thank you, Justice White. In settling cases. Pressure on both sides. On both sides. And you wanted that. I did. While it sounds rather confusing, I must say given the facts of this case. That sounds pretty plain to me. So you want us to follow up all the laws so you can do that? I do not, Justice Marshall. I do not think any law has to be filed up. But did not you file this case originally? Yes, I did, Your Honor. Did not you remand it? Yes, I did, Your Honor. You removed it, I mean? No. No, it was removed by the defendant, by Carnegie Mellon University. And so now you want it remanded? Yes, Your Honor.
